principles: Use the common frog throughout so the life cycle, habitat, colour, and call form one coherent nonfiction sequence.
Replace fixed or overgeneralised claims with accurate wording supported by amphibian conservation and natural-history sources.
Keep sentences concrete and short enough for Level C readers while retaining useful scientific vocabulary.

pages.reason: Narrows the subject to common frogs and accurately describes their freshwater and damp-land life.
pages.text: Common frogs are amphibians. They begin life in fresh water. As adults, they can live in water and on damp land.

pages.reason: Adds the spring breeding context and accurately describes common-frog spawn as clumps of jelly-coated eggs.
pages.text: In spring, female common frogs lay eggs in ponds. The eggs form clumps called frogspawn. Clear jelly surrounds each dark egg.

pages.reason: Uses the supported two-to-four-week hatching range and avoids comparing tadpoles loosely with fish.
pages.text: After two to four weeks, tadpoles hatch. They have tails and no legs. Their gills help them get oxygen from the water.

pages.reason: Keeps the correct order of limb growth and removes a misleading fixed twelve-week completion claim.
pages.text: As a tadpole grows, back legs appear first. Front legs come next. Its tail slowly becomes shorter. This change is called metamorphosis.

pages.reason: Names the froglet stage and accurately shows its short remaining tail and need for damp cover.
pages.text: A young frog is called a froglet. It has four legs and a short tail. It leaves the pond but stays near damp cover.

pages.reason: Describes common-frog feeding without the unsupported less-than-a-blink timing claim.
pages.text: Common frogs eat insects, worms, slugs, and snails. They can snap up small prey with a sticky tongue.

pages.reason: Explains moist permeable skin and breathing in concise, accurate language.
pages.text: A common frog has smooth, moist skin. It can take in oxygen through its skin. It also breathes with lungs.

pages.reason: Replaces a false general rule about bright poison colours with the real colour variation and camouflage of common frogs.
pages.text: Common frogs can be brown, olive, grey, yellow, or red. Dark patches help them blend in with mud and plants.

pages.reason: Uses the common frog's soft spring croak and explains the purpose of male calls without mixing unrelated species.
pages.text: In spring, male common frogs make soft croaking calls near the pond. Their calls help females find them. Each frog species has its own call.
